title: eBay Rejects GameStop's $56B Bid as 'Neither Credible Nor Attractive'
summary: In a David-and-Goliath twist, video game retailer GameStop made a $56 billion bid to acquire e-commerce giant eBay—and was swiftly rebuffed. eBay's board called the half-cash, half-stock proposal "neither credible nor attractive," pointing to concerns over financing and the combined company's leadership structure. The rejection underscores a stark size mismatch: eBay's market value is roughly four times GameStop's. Under CEO Jamie Iannone, eBay's stock has soared 201% over six years, and its board insists the company is on a sustainable growth path. GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen, a billionaire who built his fortune with Chewy, surprised Wall Street with the offer. He secured a $20 billion debt commitment from TD Bank, contingent on the merged entity earning an investment-grade credit rating. But eBay and sources familiar with the matter deem that unlikely. Moody's has already said the deal would be credit negative for eBay. Cohen argues that combining forces would slash costs and create a tougher rival to Amazon, leveraging GameStop's 600 U.S. stores as a physical network. Yet analysts note eBay's EBITDA margin is 31%, triple GameStop's 10%, raising doubts about the promised synergies. Cohen, who owns a 5% stake in eBay, has hinted he might appeal directly to shareholders—a difficult path requiring a larger stake to call a special meeting. The bid has captivated retail investors, who revere Cohen for his role in the 2021 GameStop short squeeze that battered hedge funds. But eBay's stock is trading far below the $125 offer price, signaling market skepticism. For now, eBay remains independent, betting on its own turnaround rather than a risky merger with a much smaller suitor.
why_it_matters: The failed bid highlights how viral enthusiasm from online communities can collide with Wall Street fundamentals—showing young people that 'meme stock' fame doesn’t automatically translate into business credibility, and that mergers require real financial logic, not just bold visions. The tug-of-war also reflects shifting power between retail investors and corporate boards, a trend that could shape future markets.

background_read: GameStop, once a mall-based video game retailer, became the center of the meme-stock craze in 2021 when a group of Reddit investors triggered a massive short squeeze—forcing hedge funds who had bet against the stock to cover their losses at skyrocketing prices.

Ryan Cohen (the founder of online pet retailer Chewy) took over GameStop in 2021 and tried to pivot the company toward e-commerce, earning a cult following among retail investors who saw him as a visionary.
eBay, launched in 1995, was one of the earliest online auction and shopping websites; it survived the dot-com bubble but has since faced stiff competition from Amazon and other platforms.

Investment-grade credit ratings (like those from Moody’s, a credit rating agency) signify low default risk; TD Bank’s $20 billion debt commitment depended on the merged company getting such a rating—something analysts and Moody’s called unlikely.
Merger proposals that are rejected can still go hostile, where the bidder tries to convince shareholders to pressure the board, but that is expensive and rare without a large toehold stake.

└─ FINANCING: The deal was half-cash, half-stock.
REJECTION REASONS: eBay’s board cited financing concerns and leadership structure issues.
├─ SIZE: eBay’s market value is about four times GameStop’s.
└─ TRACK RECORD: Under CEO Jamie Iannone, eBay’s stock rose 201% in six years, and the board insists on a sustainable growth path.
GAMESTOP’S VISION: Ryan Cohen argues a merger would slash costs and build a stronger rival to Amazon.
├─ DEBT: He secured a $20 billion commitment from TD Bank, but it required an investment-grade credit rating.
└─ DOUBT: Moody’s says the deal would be credit negative; analysts point to big gap in profitability (EBITDA margin 31% vs. 10%).
COHEN’S MANEUVER: He owns a 5% stake in eBay and may appeal directly to shareholders.
├─ FAME: Revered for the 2021 short squeeze.
└─ HURDLE: He likely needs a significantly larger stake to call a special meeting.
MARKET SKEPTICISM: eBay’s stock trades far below the $125 offer price, signaling investors don’t believe the deal will happen.
OPEN QUESTION: Whether Cohen will pursue a hostile approach or eBay will remain independent, betting on its own turnaround.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue that Cohen’s ambitious bid shows GameStop isn’t content staying a stagnant retailer. By seeking a transformative merger, he could unlock value for long-suffering shareholders and finally give eBay a new competitive edge against Amazon, benefiting both companies’ customer bases.

Critics say the bid is a reckless overreach by a far smaller company. eBay’s board correctly protected its shareholders by rejecting a deal that could saddle the firm with massive debt, a volatile stock component, and questionable synergies—especially when eBay already has a successful turnaround plan.

The episode illustrates the lasting aftershocks of the meme-stock era: charismatic CEOs with retail-investor support can pressure large corporations, but traditional valuation metrics (market cap ratios, EBITDA margins, credit ratings) still govern real-world mergers. The financing condition from Moody’s and TD Bank shows that institutional gatekeepers retain significant power.

If Cohen can increase his stake and persuade more institutional investors, a hostile proxy battle might emerge, testing shareholder democracy. Alternatively, eBay’s rejection might push GameStop to seek other, more achievable acquisitions, reshaping the retail landscape. The outcome could set a precedent for how meme-stock-driven companies challenge established players.
